input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-99: Undergraduate Cooperative Education Seminar. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This seminar helps students prepare for Computer Science co-operative education employment (“co-op”) by developing job search strategies and materials, and reviewing relevant policies. Students are introduced to RIT’s Office of Career Services and Cooperative Education, and learn about professional, legal, and ethical responsibilities for their co-op and subsequent professional experiences. Completion of this seminar and the related assignments are required before a CS student can be registered for co-op. The seminar will also review various curricular options and program requirements for CS undergraduate students. Prerequisites: This class is restricted to COMPSCI-BS or COMPEX-UND Major students with at least 2nd year standing. Contact Hours: Lecture 1 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

[rit-csci-99]
This seminar helps students prepare for Computer Science co-operative education employment (“co-op”) by developing job search strategies and materials, and reviewing relevant policies. Students are introduced to RIT’s Office of Career Services and Cooperative Education, and learn about professional, legal, and ethical responsibilities for their co-op and subsequent professional experiences. Completion of this seminar and the related assignments are required before a CS student can be registered for co-op. The seminar will also review various curricular options and program requirements for CS undergraduate students. Prerequisites: This class is restricted to COMPSCI-BS or COMPEX-UND Major students with at least 2nd year standing. Contact Hours: Lecture 1 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.visualDirection: Show a split-screen graphic: left side displays a resume template, right side shows a mock interview checklist.

beats.claim: Students are introduced to RIT’s Office of Career Services and Cooperative Education to understand institutional support structures.
beats.example: Students learn how to access career counseling, co-op placement portals, and alumni networking resources.

beats.visualDirection: Display a directory-style layout with icons for 'Career Counseling', 'Co-op Portal', and 'Alumni Network' under a central 'Office of Career Services' header.

beats.claim: Students must understand the professional, legal, and ethical responsibilities that apply to co-op and subsequent professional experiences.

beats.title: Professional, Legal, and Ethical Responsibilities
beats.visualDirection: Show a shield icon divided into three sections labeled 'Professional', 'Legal', and 'Ethical', with brief bullet points underneath each.

beats.claim: Computing professionals are directed to contribute to society, avoid harm, and maintain high standards of professional competence and ethical practice.
beats.example: Students analyze a case study where a developer must choose between meeting a tight deadline and implementing robust security measures.
beats.title: ACM Code of Ethics Foundations
beats.visualDirection: Display a circular diagram with arrows connecting 'Contribute to Society', 'Avoid Harm', 'Maintain High Standards', and 'Ethical Practice' to a central 'ACM Code' node.

beats.claim: Ethical computing decisions require identifying stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.
beats.example: Students map out a stakeholder impact chart for a proposed algorithm that processes user data, noting potential privacy risks and mitigation steps.
beats.title: Ethical Decision-Making Framework
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart starting with 'Identify Stakeholders' -> 'Assess Benefits/Harms' -> 'Evaluate Alternatives' -> 'Determine Obligations' -> 'Make Decision'.

beats.claim: Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence, cites prior work, and reports results accurately without fabrication or falsification.
beats.example: Students practice rewriting a draft abstract to separate empirical findings from theoretical hypotheses and add proper citations.
beats.title: Responsible Technical Communication
beats.visualDirection: Display a side-by-side comparison: 'Before' shows a paragraph mixing claims and evidence; 'After' shows clearly separated sections with citation markers.

beats.claim: Authors should preserve research integrity by describing methods well enough for evaluation, making limitations visible, and avoiding plagiarism.
beats.example: Students draft a methodology section that explicitly states sample sizes, tools used, and known constraints of their experimental setup.
beats.title: Research Integrity and Methodology
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist graphic with items: 'Methods Described for Evaluation', 'Limitations Disclosed', 'Plagiarism Avoided', 'Conflicts Disclosed'.

learningObjectives: Students will articulate the three core ethical responsibilities of computing professionals as defined by the ACM Code of Ethics.
Students will explain how responsible technical communication requires distinguishing claims from evidence and accurately reporting research results.
Students will identify the mandatory prerequisites and curricular requirements for registering for a Computer Science co-op program at RIT.
